courseDetails.title: Small Business Finance: Budget, Pay and Profitability
courseDetails.shortDescription: small business finance | budgeting | payroll budget | salary ranges | employee benefits | job grading | profitability
courseDetails.longDescription:
This course contains the use of artificial intelligence.

One thing to be clear about before you buy: pricing in this course means the price of work, not the price of a product. If you came for how to price what you sell, this is the wrong course.

Small businesses do not lose money on bookkeeping. They lose it on commitments

The usual finance course for a small business is bookkeeping for beginners — here is the profit and loss statement, here is the balance sheet, here is cash flow. Useful, and not where the money goes. It goes on decisions made once and then in force for years: what to pay the second person when the first one asks for a rise, whether the bonus goes to everybody or to results, whether to add insurance because a competitor did. Each of those looks like a personnel decision and is in fact a multi-year financial commitment. In a company of ten people, the payroll is the budget — and profitability is decided there rather than in the accounts.

What this course covers

Thirty-nine lessons. The model first: what an efficiency-driven business means and which measures show it, turning a strategy into financial goals, how models change from start-up to corporation, mission embedded into planned figures, process chains and the black holes inside them, goals people believe in, the strategy pyramid, planning that produces decisions rather than documents, indicators across customers, people, processes and finance without killing motivation, Lean applied to financial processes, and scaling without rebuilding every time. Then the budget built from the bottom: what can be budgeted at all, strategy before numbers, market benchmarks, the return calculation behind a request, payroll and unfilled positions, bonuses, benefits and overheads, development spending that survives a mid-year cut, and the costs nobody plans and everybody pays. Then the price of work: what companies actually pay for, the role of a salary range, analysing a job before pricing it, grading and pay structure with a ready tool, a bonus formula, the benefits system with a cafeteria plan, salary market reviews and how to use one, and recognition and referral bonuses. Then the pay system itself: compensation philosophy, grades and ranges, pay equity, the repertory grid and factorial methods, selecting grade width, linking grades to what the market pays, the pay policy, payroll budgeting, and the salary review matrix. Finally benefits and what they return: the WorldatWork model, the categories, three ways to justify the spend, flexible schemes, researching what people actually want, budgeting the package, and automation.
